headline: Roosters win a thriller in the NRL Grand Final, gold surges to $3,685 on Middle East tensions, while your portfolio holds steady with TTWO up 3% and ASX broadly higher.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: TTWO had a strong night last session, up 3.1%. The GTA 6 hype machine keeps rolling — analysts are calling it a potential 'cash cow for a decade', and even an unauthorised fan-made PC port making news is keeping the game top of mind. Long-term story remains very much intact.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: Google slipped 2% last session, extending a rough run — the stock is down about 15% over the past year despite record cloud growth. The market seems to be favouring competitors' AI narratives right now. Nothing fundamentally broken; this looks more like sentiment than substance.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft dipped 1.25% last session. News of a 24-hour service outage and a 'Code Red' security alert from CEO Satya Nadella weighed on sentiment. Short-term noise for a long-term holder — cloud growth fundamentals haven't changed.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS bounced 1.5% at today's close, a small positive after a rough stretch. However, news today highlights lithium prices are crashing again — that remains the core headwind for Pilbara. Today's move is encouraging but the bigger picture is still challenging.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI gained 1.3% today, helped by ongoing AI optimism. Data-centre power demand continues to drive holdings in AI infrastructure ETFs. The long-term AI theme is intact even if this ETF is still down nearly 20% from your cost base.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG ticked up a solid 0.67% at today's close, riding the broader ASX 200 rally of 0.8%. Nothing dramatic — just the diversified ETF doing what it's supposed to do.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS added 0.65% today on the ASX. This reflects last night's mixed US session (S&P and NASDAQ were down slightly), but the AUD-denominated ETF got a mild lift as the Aussie dollar ticked higher, partly offsetting overnight US softness.

movers.name: DHHF
movers.note: DHHF gained a quiet 0.48% today, tracking the broader market higher. Your cost and current value are almost identical — essentially flat overall, which is exactly what a broad diversified ETF looks like near entry.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE was essentially flat today, up just 0.07%. Emerging markets are caught between Middle East tensions, rising oil prices, and the ongoing Iran economic story — plenty of cross-currents keeping this one subdued.

watch_today.title: TTWO: GTA 6 hype building — hold and enjoy the ride
watch_today.detail: Take-Two jumped 3.1% last night. Analysts at Yahoo Finance are calling GTA 6 a 'cash cow for the next decade', and even fan-made PC ports going viral (before Rockstar shut them down) are keeping the game in the headlines. You're up 5.3% overall on TTWO. As a long-term holder, there's no reason to touch this — the GTA 6 launch catalyst is still ahead of you.

watch_today.title: GOOG: Down 2% last night, down 15% over the year — but hold
watch_today.detail: Google slipped another 2% last session amid concerns the market is preferring Microsoft and OpenAI's AI stories. The stock is down ~15% over the past year despite record cloud growth numbers. You're sitting at -11.86% on this position. Nothing structurally broken — Google still dominates search, YouTube, and cloud. For a long-term holder, this is a hold, not a panic.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX: Small bounce today but lithium prices crashing again
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals gained 1.5% today, which is nice — but news breaking today says lithium prices are crashing again. You're already down 60.8% on this position. The long-term lithium thesis (EVs, batteries) is intact but the timeline has blown out badly. Unless you believe deeply in the multi-year recovery story, this one deserves a close watch. Hold for now, but eyes open.

watch_today.title: Gold surging — good tailwind for broader portfolio
watch_today.detail: Gold jumped 4.2% last night to $3,685 USD/oz — a massive single-session move driven by escalating Middle East tensions (US-Iran conflict fears, Iran warning South Korea over naval deployment). This is a 'fear trade' — when investors get nervous they pile into gold. It's also pushing oil up 2.8% to $86/barrel. Watch for follow-through volatility in global markets.

watch_today.title: RBA rate outlook: no cuts expected in 2027, IMF wants rates higher
watch_today.detail: Multiple analysts are now saying the RBA (Reserve Bank of Australia — Australia's central bank) won't cut interest rates at all in 2027. On top of that, the IMF is urging the RBA to be ready to raise rates further if inflation worsens. Perth inflation hit 5.5% in October. This is a headwind for growth assets — higher rates for longer mean borrowing stays expensive and can weigh on share valuations.

watch_today.title: MSFT: 24-hour outage and security alert — short-term noise
watch_today.detail: Microsoft declared 'Code Red' after a 24-hour service outage, with CEO Satya Nadella acknowledging the floor of cyber attacks has risen. The stock fell 1.25% last night. You're still up 10.57% on MSFT overall. Cloud outages are disruptive but rarely change the long-term investment thesis for a company this size — sit tight.

world.summary: Middle East tensions are dominating world news, with fears of a full-scale US-Iran war growing, gold and oil spiking on the uncertainty. China's role as either peacemaker or profiteer is under the microscope. Meanwhile William and Kate's Sandringham home was broken into, and the Australia Under-20s soccer team pulled off an epic comeback.

stories.title: Arab officials fear return to full-scale US-Iran war
stories.why_it_matters: Senior Arab diplomats and officials are privately warning that tensions between the US and Iran are at their most dangerous level in years, and that a miscalculation could trigger a full-scale war. Iran's economy is already under severe strain from US sanctions (described as a 'silent war' by the WSJ), and Iran is now warning South Korea not to deploy naval forces to the region. For everyday Australians, this matters because it's already pushing oil prices up — higher oil means higher petrol prices and airfares. Gold is also surging as investors panic-buy safe havens.

stories.title: Iran's economy straining under US blockade — a 'Silent War'
stories.why_it_matters: The Wall Street Journal reports that Iran is experiencing what insiders are calling a 'silent war' — not from bombs, but from the crushing weight of US economic sanctions and a blockade cutting off Iranian oil exports. Inflation inside Iran is soaring, the currency is collapsing, and ordinary Iranians are struggling to afford basic goods. The concern for global markets is that a desperate Iran may become more unpredictable militarily — which is what's spooking Arab officials and driving the gold and oil rally seen overnight.

stories.title: China in the Iran conflict: Peacemaker or profiteer?
stories.why_it_matters: Australia's Lowy Institute — a leading foreign policy think tank — has published an analysis asking whether China is genuinely trying to broker peace between the US and Iran, or quietly benefiting from the chaos by buying cheap sanctioned Iranian oil and expanding its Middle East influence. This matters for Australia because China is our biggest trading partner, and anything that shifts the US-China dynamic in the Middle East ripples through to our trade relationships, commodity prices, and regional security.

stories.title: Soaring jet fuel prices are eroding global airline profits
stories.why_it_matters: With oil prices spiking due to Middle East conflict, jet fuel costs — which are directly derived from crude oil — are surging and biting deeply into airline profits globally. Airlines are caught between higher costs and reluctance to fully pass them on to passengers for fear of killing demand. If you're planning travel, this is a warning sign that airfares may rise. For investors, airlines and travel stocks are in the crosshairs.

stories.title: Major security probe after break-in at William and Kate's Sandringham estate
stories.why_it_matters: Someone broke into the Sandringham estate in Norfolk — the country home of Prince William and Princess Kate — triggering a major security review by royal protection officers. The intruder reportedly accessed part of the grounds before being detected. No one was harmed, but the incident has exposed gaps in the security arrangements for one of the Royal Family's most private properties, raising serious questions about how well the royals are protected outside of central London.

markets.summary: The ASX 200 had a good day, closing up 0.8% to 8,834 — a solid session. Last night in the US, the S&P 500 and NASDAQ both slipped slightly (down 0.25% and 0.62% respectively) as investors weighed Middle East tensions. The big movers were gold — up 4.2% to $3,685 — and oil, up 2.8% to $86/barrel, both driven by fears of escalating US-Iran conflict. The Aussie dollar ticked up slightly to 66.7 US cents.

indicators.note: Strong session today — up 0.8% to close near 8,834.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's session — slipped mildly, down 0.25% to 7,183.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Last night — down 0.62%, tech stocks under mild pressure.

indicators.name: Gold (WTI)
indicators.note: Massive jump — up 4.2% as Middle East tensions drive safe-haven buying.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Up 2.8% — Iran conflict fears pushing oil higher. Watch petrol prices.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: Aussie dollar nudged higher — up 0.6% to 66.7 US cents.

politics.summary: The RBA and interest rates are dominating Australian economic news today, with analysts, economists, and the IMF all weighing in — and none of it is great news for borrowers. Labor is also making moves on trust tax rules and superannuation advice laws.

stories.title: No RBA rate cuts expected in 2027, and the IMF wants rates to go higher
stories.why_it_matters: Multiple analysts are now saying the RBA (Reserve Bank of Australia — our central bank) will not cut interest rates at any point during 2027. On top of that, the IMF is publicly urging the RBA to be ready to raise rates again if inflation gets worse. Perth's inflation hit 5.5% in October, adding pressure. For everyday Australians with mortgages, this means high repayments are here to stay for even longer than hoped. For investors, 'higher for longer' rates can weigh on the value of growth stocks and property.

stories.title: SMH opinion: RBA is 'punishing the wrong Australians' and must cut now
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Morning Herald is running a pointed opinion piece arguing the RBA has 'forgotten its job' and is hitting renters, low-income workers, and younger Australians hardest with high rates, while wealthier property owners benefit from rising asset prices. The piece argues for immediate rate cuts. This reflects a growing public and political debate about who actually bears the pain of the RBA's inflation fight — expect this to become a hot-button issue heading into any upcoming election cycle.

stories.title: Labor's trust tax change — what it means for family wills
stories.why_it_matters: Labor is making changes to how family trusts are taxed, particularly around distributions made via wills and estate planning. The changes affect how income split through discretionary trusts (a common structure used by small business owners and wealthy families to minimise tax) is treated on death. If your family uses a trust structure for investment or business purposes, this is worth talking to your accountant about — the rules are tightening.

stories.title: Albanese government secures Greens support for three major reforms
stories.why_it_matters: The Albanese government has locked in Greens support to pass three significant reforms through parliament. While specific details weren't available from the article text, securing Greens votes is typically tied to concessions on climate, housing, or social policy. This gives Labor a path to pass legislation it couldn't get through on its own — a notable political development as the government looks to cement its second-term agenda.

ai.summary: OpenAI is pulling ahead in the humanoid robotics race, Chinese AI developers are facing delays that benefit Western rivals, and US Congress is struggling to agree on how to regulate AI at all.

stories.title: OpenAI beats Google and Anthropic in humanoid robot benchmark
stories.why_it_matters: OpenAI has topped a new benchmark test for AI systems controlling humanoid robots — beating Google's DeepMind and Anthropic's Claude-based systems. The benchmark tests how well an AI can control a human-shaped robot doing real-world physical tasks. This is significant because it shows OpenAI isn't just winning the chatbot race — it's building towards AI that can operate in the physical world, which is where the really big commercial opportunity lies (manufacturing, logistics, aged care). Your GXAI.AX ETF holds companies in this space.

stories.title: Chinese AI developers facing delays — breathing room for OpenAI, Google, Anthropic
stories.why_it_matters: Leading Chinese AI labs are reportedly facing significant delays in their next-generation model releases, partly due to US chip export restrictions cutting off access to Nvidia's most powerful GPUs. This gives Western AI giants — OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic — more runway to establish dominance before serious Chinese competition arrives. Good news for GOOG and MSFT holders — both companies have massive AI investments that benefit from reduced competitive pressure.

stories.title: US Congress can't agree on how to regulate AI
stories.why_it_matters: The New York Times reports that despite broad agreement in Congress that AI needs some form of regulation, lawmakers are deeply divided on what that actually looks like — and lobbyists from major tech companies are exploiting that division to block meaningful rules. The key sticking points are whether to regulate AI models themselves, the applications built on them, or just specific 'high-risk' uses. For investors, regulatory uncertainty is a double-edged sword: it removes the risk of heavy-handed rules slowing growth, but it also means the industry is operating without guardrails, which creates liability risk down the track.

stories.title: ChatGPT vs Gemini vs Claude: Who's winning in November 2026?
stories.why_it_matters: An Analytics Insight analysis looking at where the three major AI assistants stand in November 2026 — ChatGPT (OpenAI), Gemini (Google), and Claude (Anthropic). Google's Gemini is fighting hard to keep up with ChatGPT, particularly on multimodal tasks (meaning tasks that combine text, images, and audio). The race is still very close at the top. Relevant for GOOG holders — Gemini's performance is central to Google's ability to monetise its AI investment and justify the stock's current valuation.

sport.summary: The Roosters won the NRL Grand Final in an absolute nail-biter, beating the Knights 19-18. The PNG Chiefs are on a massive signing spree ahead of their NRL debut. World No.1 tennis player Jannik Sinner has been ruled out of the Australian Open after knee surgery. And there's AFL off-season chaos with player movements and a Collingwood big name walking out.

stories.title: ROOSTERS WIN THE NRL GRAND FINAL 19-18 — Knight heartbreak in Sydney
stories.why_it_matters: In one of the greatest Grand Finals in recent memory, the Sydney Roosters defeated the Newcastle Knights 19-18 at Accor Stadium on Sunday night. It was a one-point thriller — the Knights will be devastated. The Roosters take home their latest premiership in a game that came down to the wire. If you watched it, you know — absolutely gripping footy.

stories.title: NRL beefs up hip-drop tackle penalties for 2027
stories.why_it_matters: The NRL has announced it will increase penalties for hip-drop tackles in 2027, responding to player safety concerns after a string of serious injuries caused by the technique. The controversial set restart rule — which hands possession back to the attacking team after certain infringements — will be retained despite debate. The hip-drop crackdown has been welcomed by players and clubs but Dragons coach has warned that banning wrestling coaches from the bench could actually lead to more concussions, not fewer.

stories.title: PNG Chiefs on a massive spending spree — Sam Walker, Maroons star signed
stories.why_it_matters: Papua New Guinea's new NRL franchise, the PNG Chiefs, are pulling off a string of high-profile signings ahead of their competition debut. Latest confirmed deals include premiership-winning Roosters halfback Sam Walker locked in for 2028, a Queensland State of Origin back-rower, and a Maroons star. The Chiefs are clearly signalling they intend to be competitive quickly, not just making up numbers. The PNG market is passionate about rugby league — this expansion is a big deal for the sport's Pacific growth.

stories.title: Jannik Sinner ruled out of Australian Open after knee surgery
stories.why_it_matters: World No. 1 and two-time Australian Open champion Jannik Sinner has been ruled out of the upcoming Australian Open after undergoing knee surgery. This is a massive blow for Tennis Australia and the event — Sinner was the defending champion and overwhelming favourite. His absence opens the draw wide open and will inevitably affect ticket demand and TV ratings for the January tournament. With the AO right here on Australian soil, this will be felt.

stories.title: Collingwood heavyweight leaves club after reported tension with coach
stories.why_it_matters: A senior Collingwood figure has departed the club following reported tensions with premiership coach Craig McRae. Fox Sports reports the split came after a breakdown in the working relationship, though the specific individual isn't named in the available details. This is part of a broader AFL off-season reshuffle — Hawthorn have also poached a Hawks father-son prospect from an interstate rival, and the Blues have signed a rookie with ties to Eddie Betts. The AFL player market is moving fast.
